text: Alisher Burkhanovich Usmanov, born on 9 September 1953 in Chust, Uzbekistan, is a Russian-Uzbek businessman widely regarded as a Russian oligarch. According to Forbes, he is the 149th richest person in the world with a net worth of $16.8 billion, primarily due to his 49% ownership stake in Metalloinvest. Usmanov was active as an entrepreneur in the Soviet Union during the 1980s but significantly expanded his wealth after the Soviet Union's collapse through investments in metal and mining operations and early investments in technology companies such as Facebook, Twitter, VK, and Alibaba Group. He owns the Kommersant publishing house, is a co-owner of MegaFon, a mobile telephone operator, and co-owner of the Udokan mine, which develops one of the world's largest copper deposits. He served as president of the Fédération Internationale d'Escrime (FIE), the international governing body of fencing, from 2008, and was re-elected in 2012 and 2016, with acclamation in 2021 for a fourth term. In 2022 and again in 2024 after his re-election, he temporarily suspended his duties due to international sanctions imposed on him by the US, EU, UK, and Ukrainian governments following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. From 1980 to 1986, he was imprisoned in a remote Uzbek prison for six years on charges of fraud, corruption, and theft of state property, including shaking down an Army officer, though his conviction was later overturned in 2000 by the Supreme Court of Uzbekistan, which ruled that the case was fabricated and no crime was committed. He was born in Chust and spent his childhood in Tashkent, where his father was a state prosecutor and his mother, Dilbar, taught Russian. Planning to become a diplomat, he studied international law at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations, graduating in 1976, and later worked in Tashkent as director of the Foreign Economic Association of the Soviet Peace Committee. He became a dollar millionaire before the Soviet Union collapsed and established Agroplast, a for-profit company producing plastic bags during a time of scarcity. After the Soviet collapse, he enriched himself through business ventures, though he consistently denied participating in the privatization of state property. He held various leadership roles in Russian enterprises, including Deputy General Director of Intercross JSC (1990–1994), head of Interfin Interbank Investment and Finance Company (1994–1998), adviser to Moscow Aviation Industrial Enterprise (1994–1995), First Deputy Chairman of MAPO-Bank (1995–1997), and First Deputy General Director of Gazprom Vestholding LLC (November 1998 to February 2000), and later served as advisor to Gazprom’s chairman (November 2000 to July 2001) and as general director of Gazprom Vestholding LLC (February 2000 to October 2014), during which he helped Gazprom acquire Severneftegazprom, controlling stakes in Zapsibgazprom and Sibur, and over 50% of Stroytransgaz. In 1999, he co-founded Metalloinvest with Vasily Anisimov, building it through secondary market acquisitions rather than privatization schemes. Metalloinvest owns Lebedinsky GOK, Mikhailovsky GOK, Oskol Elektrometallurgical Plant, Ural Steel steel mills, and Ural Scrap Company. In March 2022, Metalloinvest sold Ural Steel to Zagorsk Pipe Plant. Usmanov holds a 49% share in USM, a global conglomerate with major investments in metals and mining, telecommunications, and technology. Between 2006 and 2008, he acquired stakes in Australian mining companies Strike Resources, Medusa, Mt Gibson, and Aztec Resources through Gallagher Holdings; in 2013, USM Holdings was formed after a merger with assets from Andrei Skoch and Farhad Moshiri. In 2009, Metalloinvest sold its 10.37% stake in Medusa Mining for A$56 million and was the second-largest shareholder in Nautilus Minerals after Mohammed Al Bawani, later taking control after the company filed for bankruptcy in 2019. In November 2015, USM invested $100 million in the esports team Virtus Pro. In 2021, USM and Metalloinvest announced plans to build one of the world's largest Hot-briquetted iron eco-plants in Kursk Oblast to supply greener steel. In 2008, Metalloinvest bought the Udokan copper licence for $500 million, discovered during Soviet times and estimated to contain 26.7 million tonnes of copper ore under JORC classification. In 2020, Baikal Mining Company (rebranded to Udokan copper) began strip mining at the site, untouched since 1949, with plans to produce up to 125,000 tonnes of copper per year and 12 million tonnes of ore. In 2008, Usmanov became acquainted with Yuri Milner and became a shareholder of DST Global and VK. He held 25.3% of interest in VK and 60.6% of voting interest until selling a $530 million stake in 2013, reducing his interest to 17.9% and 58.1%. In 2013, through VK, he acquired Pavel Durov's shares in Vk.ru to help Durov retain control of Telegram when UCP attempted to take over. In December 2021, he sold his VK interests to Sogaz, a state-run insurer with Gazprom as its largest shareholder, claiming he was exiting at the peak. In May 2008, he acquired a majority interest in MegaFon, holding 49% through USM. In 2009, Usmanov invested $200 million in Facebook via Mail.ru, receiving a 1.96% stake that valued Facebook at $10 billion, without voting rights, and netted $1.4 billion from the sale in 2013. In 2011, DST Global invested $400 million in Twitter for 5%, which was sold in 2014. Through Mail.ru, he invested in Groupon, Zynga, Airbnb, Zocdoc, Xiaomi, Alibaba Group, and JD.com. In 2013, he invested $100 million in Apple and sold his shares in early 2014. In September 2018, Mail.ru entered a $2 billion joint venture with Alibaba to merge online marketplaces in Russia, backed by the Kremlin via the Russian Direct Investment Fund. In August 2006, he bought Kommersant for $200 million, a newspaper formerly owned by Boris Berezovsky, and also purchased a 50% stake in 7TV for $25 million in November 2006 and 75% of Muz-TV for $300 million in June 2007; a stake in Muz-TV was sold to Walt Disney in 2011 for $300 million. He sold his TV assets to business partner Ivan Tavrin in 2017. In 2012, Usmanov announced plans to retire at age 63, which he implemented in 2014 by stepping down from active management and shifting focus to philanthropy, including promoting Uzbekistan’s development and sports. In 2023, he resigned from the board of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs. In 2020, he stated in an interview with the Financial Times that he would leave his assets to his family and USM management, allocating 50% to family and 50% to management. Usmanov was a shareholder of Arsenal Football Club from 2007 to 2018, acquiring a 14.58% stake in August 2007 for £75 million with business partner Farhad Moshiri from David Dein. His investment vehicle, Red and White Holdings, increased its stake to 23% in September 2007, over 24% in February 2008, 25% in February 2009, and confirmed as the club’s largest shareholder outside the board. A "lock-down" agreement was implemented by the club’s board, restricting share sales to "permitted persons" until April 2009 and requiring board members to have first option on shares until October 2012. American businessman Stan Kroenke increased his stake to over 62% in April 2011, becoming majority shareholder and required to make a buyout offer, which Usmanov refused. Usmanov increased his stake beyond 29% in June 2011 and purchased shares from Rangers in February 2012, owning over 30% by October 2013. He criticized Arsenal’s lack of ambition and financial model in a letter to the board in July 2012 and maintained his stake. In August 2018, he sold his Arsenal shares to Kroenke for £550 million. In January 2017, USM entered a five-year, $15 million+ deal with Everton F.C. for naming rights to its training ground, Finch Farm. Farhad Moshiri, Usmanov’s accountant and partner in USM, was formerly the majority shareholder of Everton and co-owner of Arsenal shares. In 2019, Megafon became Everton’s sleeve sponsor for men’s training wear and official matchday presenting partner, and in 2020 expanded to become the main sponsor of the women’s team. Despite being barred from entering the UK in 2021, companies linked to Usmanov continued to fund Everton. In March 2022, Everton suspended its sponsorship with USM and MegaFon due to the Russian invasion of Ukraine. A former sabre fencer for the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic, Usmanov supported fencing through his charity fund "For the Future of Fencing," created in 2004. Media estimates indicate his total donations to the FIE during his tenure as president amount to approximately $100 million. He was president of the Russian Fencing Federation from 2001 to 2009 and the European Fencing Confederation from 2005 to 2009. He was elected FIE president in 2008 with 66 votes to 61 for René Roch, re-elected in 2012 and 2016, and by acclamation in 2021. During his presidency, he expanded the Olympic fencing programme to 12 disciplines. Following sanctions, he announced on 1 March 2022 that he would step down as FIE president, suspending his duties with Emmanuel Katsiadakis serving as interim president. On 30 November 2024, he was re-elected for a new term and again suspended his duties, with Katsiadakis appointed interim president. In February 2008, Metalloinvest became sponsor of FC Dynamo Moscow, replacing Xerox Corporation in a $7 million deal. Usmanov was a member of the Councils of the 2014 Sochi XXII Olympic Winter Games and XI Paralympic Winter Games and is a member of the Board of Trustees of the Russian Olympian Sportsmen Support Fund.

A number of initiatives, including the expansion of the Olympic fencing programme to 12 disciplines, were implemented. Following the imposition of sanctions on Alisher Usmanov, he announced on 1 March 2022 that he was stepping down as FIE President, though he did not resign but suspended himself, with Emmanuel Katsiadakis serving as Interim President. On 30 November 2024, Usmanov was re-elected for a new term as President and suspended himself again, with Katsiadakis appointed Interim President once more. In February 2008, Metalloinvest became sponsor of FC Dynamo Moscow, replacing Xerox Corporation on players' shirts under a $7 million deal. Usmanov was a member of the Councils of the 2014 Sochi XXII Olympic Winter Games and XI Paralympic Winter Games and is also a member of the Board of Trustees of the Russian Olympian Sportsmen Support Fund. In 2015, USM invested the equivalent of US$100 million in the Eastern European eSports team Virtus.pro. On 2 September 2007, former British Ambassador Craig Murray claimed Usmanov was a gangster and racketeer who served six years in jail, with his pardon orchestrated by Uzbekistan President Islam Karimov under instructions from power broker Gafur Rakhimov, and that Usmanov paid a $88 million bribe to Gulnara Karimova, the daughter of Karimov; Murray also alleged Usmanov was involved in a covered-up rape and the death of a journalist. The Mail on Sunday re-published these allegations in December 2007, leading Usmanov, represented by Schillings, to threaten libel, prompting the newspaper to apologize and remove the article, which was later taken down by Murray's web host under pressure from Schillings. Schillings warned independent blog owners to remove references to Murray’s allegations and any reproduction of his blog post. Indymedia received take-down notices on 10 and 21 September 2007, and unrelated political blogs hosted on the same server, including those by Boris Johnson and Bloggerheads.com, suffered downtime. On 12 December 2011, Kommersant Vlast magazine published an unflattering issue titled "Victory of United ballot-stuffers" featuring a ballot with "Putin, go fuck yourself" scrawled in red ink, leading Usmanov to fire editor Maxim Kovalsky and publisher head Andrei Galiyev for an "ethical breach" and "petty hooliganism." Demyan Kudryavtsev, head of Kommersant, resigned, stating the issue violated internal procedures, journalistic standards, and Russian law. Nadezhda Azhgihina, executive secretary of the Russian Union of Journalists, called the incident "a clear example of censorship from the owner." On 14 December 2011, 60 journalists signed an open letter to Usmanov, criticizing the dismissal as intimidation and accusing it of suppressing criticism of Vladimir Putin. Usmanov responded that he could understand the journalists' stance but maintained Kommersant Vlast was a respectable, independent publication. Mikhail Prokhorov, who had announced a 2012 presidential candidacy, offered to buy Kommersant on the same day, but Usmanov rejected the offer. In 2013, Kovalsky returned to Kommersant and worked until his death from cancer in 2019. Despite sanctions on Usmanov by the U.S. Department of Treasury, OFAC issued General License No. 64 to authorize transactions "ordinarily incident and necessary to the operations of the newspaper Kommersant," which U.S. officials consider one of the last independent media outlets in Russia. However, due to vague wording in the license, almost all of Kommersant's international partners ceased cooperation, resulting in loss of access to tools like the Bloomberg Terminal and disconnection from Google Discover, which accounted for nearly 40% of daily clicks. In 2012, Usmanov hired London-based PR firm RLM Finsbury to edit his Wikipedia article to remove information on his criminal convictions and controversies; the CEO of the Chartered Institute of Public Relations stated that PR professionals should not directly edit Wikipedia for clients, and the firm claimed it acted without Usmanov’s authorization, with the edits made in expectation of MegaFon’s stock market listing. In 2004, Usmanov acquired 13% of Corus Group (later Tata Steel Europe), borrowing $49.5 million from Sevenkey, a trust for Igor Shuvalov, top assistant to Vladimir Putin, with funds provided by Eugene Shvidler; Sevenkey received over 40% annualized return, and in 2006 received 4.9% of Gallagher’s investment income. In 2018, U.S. Senators Marco Rubio, Roger Wicker, Lindsey Graham, and Cory Gardner called on the Trump administration to sanction Usmanov for alleged corruption and bribery of Russian government officials. In June 2024, Usmanov sued UBS for submitting "unsubstantiated reports" about his transactions, triggering a money laundering investigation by German authorities; he claimed the bank violated confidentiality agreements by sharing more than a dozen misleading reports from 2018 to 2022 with German police. In November 2024, he paid €4 million in fines and charitable donations to settle the investigation without admitting guilt. Usmanov’s lawyers stated that after over two-and-a-half years, the investigation failed to prove the accusations. In February 2022, in response to the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the European Union designated Usmanov, imposing a travel ban and freezing all his assets. In March 2022, the United States imposed similar sanctions, with exceptions for companies in which Usmanov directly or indirectly held stakes, and the British government also sanctioned him. In March 2024, Swedish economist Anders Åslund removed his post on X where he called Usmanov one of "Putin’s favourite oligarchs" at Usmanov’s request, which was used by the Council as justification for sanctions. Usmanov denied the allegations and filed an appeal in the EU General Court, which was dismissed on 7 February 2024. However, the EU Council dropped the term "oligarch" from the sanctions reasoning, now referring to Usmanov as a "leading businessperson." According to the Index, Usmanov's net worth fell by nearly 25% from 22 February to 15 March 2022 due to sanctions. Usmanov was named in the Official Journal of the European Union as a "leading businessperson having interests in iron ore and steel, media, telecommunications and internet companies," described as one of Vladimir Putin’s favourite leading businesspersons and considered one of Russia’s businesspersons-officials entrusted with servicing financial flows whose positions depend on the President’s will. Usmanov claimed the sanctions were based on false and defamatory allegations and filed a lawsuit in the EU Court to prove the accusations invalid and lift the sanctions, asserting his fame and fortune, not links to Putin, made him a target. His lawyers argued he was unfairly targeted as "prey" because he was a "visible symbol" known to the public. In August 2025, German lawyer Joachim Steinhöfel filed a defamation lawsuit against the EU Council, accusing it of introducing sanctions based on unfounded journalist allegations. On 3 September 2025, the EU General Court dismissed Usmanov’s de-listing application, noting his stake in USM is "non-controlling." Usmanov also sued Forbes for an article containing allegations that formed the basis of sanctions; his lawyers successfully proved the allegations were defamatory and unfounded. In March 2022, the German Cabinet established a task force to track Usmanov’s funds and assets, involving the Ministry of Economics and Finance, BaFin, the Federal Criminal Police Office, customs, and the Federal Intelligence Service (BND). The Federal Criminal Police Office identified 36 offshore companies and 90 suspicious money laundering reports linked to Usmanov. Usmanov denied all accusations, arguing under the Russia-Germany double taxation agreement he did not have to pay taxes in Germany because all taxes were paid in Russia, a claim refuted in numerous court proceedings. Usmanov does not own any real estate in Germany; all properties are held in irrevocable family trusts prior to sanctions. On 12 May 2023, the Land Court in Frankfurt am Main invalidated and annulled search orders for properties linked to Usmanov, including villas on Lake Tegernsee, an apartment in Frankfurt, and other properties, as well as the Dilbar yacht in Bremen, declaring the searches illegal, the accusations of money laundering groundless, and citing numerous formal violations. German media called the case "the investigators' disgrace." Another search occurred in early October 2023. On 26 October 2023, the court ordered the return of property seized during searches. Searches with document seizures also occurred at the football club Bavaria’s office and Allianz Arena, with the search authorization later withdrawn and documents returned. In June 2023, Usmanov submitted a complaint to the German Constitutional Court, alleging violations of fundamental rights under the Basic Law and the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, seeking to declare provisions of the German Foreign Trade Act unconstitutional, particularly those requiring sanctioned individuals to report their assets, which he claims violates the constitutional privilege against self-incrimination. He also sought recognition of searches on the Dilbar yacht as violations of the inviolability of the dwelling and personal dignity. Usmanov’s sister, Gulbakhor Ismailova, was the beneficiary of the trust owning the Dilbar yacht before sanctions; in March 2024, she irrevocably and permanently waived all rights to family trust benefits. In March 2025, the EU removed Ismailova from its 2000-person sanctions list as part of a deal with Hungary, which had threatened to veto the sanctions framework. Another sister, Saodat Narzieva, was on the EU sanctions list, but after investigations proved that data from "Suisse Secrets" claiming she was the beneficial owner of up to 27 Credit Suisse accounts was false, the EU lifted sanctions from her on 14 September 2022. In October 2023, the German Central Office for Sanctions Enforcement (ZfS) searched several properties in the Munich area and on Lake Tegernsee, with around 30 investigators searching a villa wrongly attributed to Usmanov and confiscating luxury vehicles and assets. Usmanov’s spokesman stated there were no reasons for suspicion, as the properties are held in a trust he does not own or control. A German court later confirmed the allegations were false and banned media from naming Usmanov as the owner of the villa. In June 2024, Usmanov filed a lawsuit against UBS Europe SE in Frankfurt over what his lawyers described as unsubstantiated reports that triggered an illegal criminal probe into his business dealings, claiming the bank violated confidentiality agreements by sharing more than a dozen misleading reports from 2018 to 2022 with German police. In November 2024, the Prosecutor General’s Office in Frankfurt am Main dropped its investigation into Usmanov. Usmanov voluntarily donated €4 million split between charities and the state, with the closure of the case not constituting an admission of guilt. Usmanov’s lawyers stated that after over two-and-a-half years, the investigation failed to prove the accusations. On 5 May 2025, the Regional Court of Hamburg ruled that the statement that Alisher Usmanov is the owner of the yacht Dilbar is false and prohibited its dissemination. At the end of 2025, the Munich II Public Prosecutor's Office dropped the case against Usmanov on suspicion of two violations of the Foreign Trade Act and possible sanctions violations in exchange for a payment of €10 million. Usmanov agreed to the dismissal by paying the sum. In September 2022, Hungary demanded the lifting of EU sanctions from Usmanov. In November 2022, the Uzbek government lobbied the EU to lift sanctions, stating they restricted Usmanov’s ability to invest in Uzbekistan. In December 2022, a Ukrainian court ordered the seizure of ₴2 billion (US$54 million) worth of USM assets, comprising 160,000 tonnes of Ukrainian iron ore. Metalloinvest denied the claim, stating Ukrainian authorities arrested iron ore produced by its enterprises in Russia and intended for export, which were blocked in February 2022. Metalloinvest warned it would take legal action against Ukraine and any potential buyer if Kyiv confiscated the iron. On 25 September 2022, Ukraine’s High Anti-Corruption Court upheld the decision to confiscate the iron-ore assets, calling it a "flagrant example of the unlawful and unfounded 'legalization' of the appropriation of private property."

In November 2022, the Uzbek government urged the EU to remove sanctions on Usmanov, arguing that they hindered his ability to invest in Uzbekistan. In December 2022, a Ukrainian court ordered the seizure of ₴2 billion (US$54 million) worth of USM assets, consisting of 160,000 tonnes of Ukrainian iron ore. Metalloinvest denied the claim, stating that the iron ore was produced by its Russian enterprises, blocked for export in February 2022, and arrested by Ukrainian authorities. The company warned it would pursue legal action against Ukraine and any potential buyer if the iron were confiscated. On September 25, Ukraine’s High Anti-Corruption Court upheld the confiscation, with USM criticizing the decision as an unlawful and unfounded seizure of private property, held illegally for over two years, and vowed to seek international judicial review. Usmanov, of Muslim heritage, married Jewish rhythmic gymnastics coach Irina Viner in 1992; Viner is considered close to Putin, having introduced him to Alina Kabaeva, now Putin’s most famous mistress. The couple divorced on July 4, 2022. Usmanov has no biological children but has a stepson, Anton Viner, with Irina, who is a real-estate investor and co-owner of the Rodina development group. Usmanov, who now resides in Tashkent, is married to Shavkat Mirziyoyev, the President of Uzbekistan, and has been credited with helping Mirziyoyev consolidate power. In 2012, Usmanov spent up to $500 million on an Airbus A340 named Bourkhan after his father. In 2004, he purchased Sutton Place, a Grade I listed Tudor mansion in Surrey covering 120 hectares (300 acres) for £10 million; Boris Berezovsky claimed it was given to Usmanov as part of a business deal, which Usmanov denied. In 2008, Usmanov bought Beechwood House, a Grade II listed Regency property in Highgate, 4.5 hectares (11 acres) in size, from Qatari sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani for £48 million. These properties are currently held in a discretionary irrevocable trust established by Usmanov. He also owns a 12-hectare (30-acre) property in Moscow and a villa on Sardinia. Usmanov allegedly owns three superyachts named Dilbar, after his mother. In 2005, he took delivery of the first Dilbar (now Luna B) from Oceanco for $60 million; a second Dilbar (now Al Raya) was delivered by Lürssen in 2008 for $250 million, making it the 38th largest motor yacht by length at 110.0 meters (361 feet) as of 2019. In 2015, he commissioned the third Dilbar, the largest yacht by gross tonnage (15,917 gt) and the 6th largest by length (156.0 meters or 512 feet), costing $800 million, employing 84 full-time crew, and featuring an 180 cubic meter indoor swimming pool. After receiving the second Dilbar, Usmanov renamed the original Ona and sold it in 2010; later, when the second Dilbar was renamed Ona, it was sold to a Middle Eastern buyer in 2018. Usmanov and his representatives claim the yacht was transferred into a family trust years ago. On March 2, 2022, German authorities seized Dilbar in Hamburg as part of sanctions against Usmanov following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. On April 15, 2022, German officials seized the yacht after investigations revealed it belonged to a trust with a former beneficiary being Usmanov’s sister, who was also sanctioned. In March 2024, Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) removed posts on X naming Ismailova as Dilbar’s owner. In February 2025, Germany’s dpa news agency, which had reported that Usmanov’s sister Gulbahor Ismailova owned Dilbar, withdrew the report as false. Media reports indicate Usmanov has donated approximately $7.3 billion to charity. In 2021, The Sunday Times named him the most generous philanthropist on its Rich List, citing donations exceeding £4.2 billion over 20 years. In 2012, Russian Forbes named him Philanthropist of the Year. In 2006, Usmanov founded the "Art, Science and Sport" Charity Fund, which supported exhibitions at Tate Britain, including the J. M. W. Turner exhibition in 2008 and the Pre-Raphaelites exhibition in 2013. He serves as a Trustee for the Russian Geographical Society, Moscow State Institute of International Relations, National Research University Higher School of Economics, and the European University at St Petersburg. In 2015, he donated €1.5 million to restore the Basilica Ulpia in Rome. In February 2020, Usmanov purchased Pierre de Coubertin’s original 1892 Olympic Manifesto for $8.8 million, donating it to the Olympic Museum, making it the world’s most expensive piece of sports memorabilia. In 2020 and 2021, Usmanov topped the list of COVID-19 donors among The Sunday Times Rich List, contributing £134.2 million to Russia, Uzbekistan, and Italy. On September 17, 2007, Usmanov paid over £20 million for an art collection from Mstislav Rostropovich, which he donated to the Russian state and housed in the Konstantinovsky Palace near St. Petersburg. That same month, he acquired rights to a Soviet cartoon collection previously owned by Oleg Vidov, valued at $5 to $10 million, which he donated to a new Russian children’s television channel. By presidential decree No. 365 of March 17, 2004, Usmanov was awarded the Medal of Honor of Russia. In 2011, he received the Order "Dostyk" (Friendship) 2nd degree from Kazakhstan. In 2013, he was awarded the Order for Service to the Fatherland IV class and a medal "For contribution to international cooperation" by the Russian Foreign Ministry. In 2014, he received the Order of Alexander Nevsky for community and charitable work. In 2016, he received the Decoration "For Beneficence" and the Al-Fahr Order for reviving Islam in Russia. In 2017, he was awarded the Commander "Order of Merit of the Italian Republic" for architectural restoration projects, presented by Italian President Sergio Mattarella. In 2018, he received the Order "For Merit to the Fatherland" 3rd class and the Order "Dostyk" 1st degree (Kazakhstan) for cultural development and strengthening international ties. In 2018, he also received the Order of El-Yurt Hurmati "Respected by people and homeland" (Uzbekistan) for major investments, creating spiritual and educational complexes, supporting sports and tourism, and being a role model for youth. On December 4, 2014, Usmanov paid $4.8 million for Dr. James Watson’s Nobel Prize Medal in Physiology or Medicine, auctioned at Christie’s in New York. After auction fees, Watson received $4.1 million. Usmanov returned the medal to Watson, stating that it was unacceptable for a scientist to sell a medal recognizing his achievements, as Watson’s work contributed to cancer research, the illness from which his father died, and emphasizing that the funds should support scientific research and the medal remain with Watson.
